extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of modern history
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from a popular early-20th-century synthetic history (H. G. Wells) discussing social, religious, scientific, and political developments and their consequences. Intended as narrative exposition and interpretation rather than a formal guideline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for constructive alternative when denouncing governments
rubrics_metrics.description: It produces little or no permanent effect to denounce a government or a world system unless you have a working idea of a better government and a better system to replace it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells emphasizes that mere denunciation is ineffective: political critique must be paired with practical, articulated alternatives (a 'working idea') to produce change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Socialist political end and consistent practice
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is any logic about the Marxist, it should be his declared political end for which he should work without ceasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes socialists who speak of the 'State' without recognizing its variety and who lack focused, persistent work toward their declared political ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historians should balance caution and boldness; restrain opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Now, upon that matter the teller of modern history is obliged to be at once cautious and bold. He has to pick his way between cowardly evasion on the one hand, and partisanship on the other. As far as possible he must confine himself to facts and restrain his opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells prescribes a historian's methodological stance: prioritize facts, avoid partisan polemic, yet acknowledge that complete suppression of opinion is impossible; be explicit about one's persuasions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historian's remit: record facts, not theological ultimate significance
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not the business of the historian to controvert or explain these matters; the question of their ultimate significance depends upon the theologian; the historian’s concern is merely with the fact that official Christianity throughout the world adopted St. Paul’s view...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish descriptive-historical claims (what happened, what was adopted) from normative/theological interpretation; historians should document institutional beliefs and developments rather than adjudicate doctrinal truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religions must adapt to scientific discoveries or lose moral authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery of man’s descent from sub-human forms does not even remotely touch the teaching of the Kingdom of Heaven. Yet priests and bishops raged at Darwin; foolish attempts were made to suppress Darwinian literature... In the end men may discover that religion shines all the brighter for the loss of its doctrinal wrappings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells argues that failure to integrate scientific findings into religious expression undermines institutional credibility and that a simplified, reformed religious statement could retain moral force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific evidence (geology, biology) undermines literal cosmogony
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole world was littered... with evidence of its utter absurdity [of literal creation dating]. ... the systematic study of geology assumed such proportions as to affect the general authority of the Bible version...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical geological and biological findings contradicted literal readings of sacred texts, forcing reinterpretation or loss of doctrinal authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of misusing scientific theories for social policy (Social Darwinism)
rubrics_metrics.description: A crude misunderstanding of Darwinism had become the fundamental mindstuff of great masses of the 'educated' everywhere... they believed that they prevailed by virtue of the Struggle for Existence... and that they had to be strong, energetic, ruthless, 'practical', egotistical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells warns that extrapolating biological theories to justify social hierarchies or cruelty is a misuse with harmful moral and political consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical/technological revolution increases need for planned, global organization
rubrics_metrics.description: An enormous amount of intellectual toil and discussion and education and many years... must intervene before a new order, planned as ships and railways are planned... runs over the whole surface of our earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because technological interdependence binds the globe, Wells asserts a practical need for large-scale, organized planning (e.g., international systems) to avoid chaos and disaster.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of governments rests on openness, truth, and legality
rubrics_metrics.description: The true strength of rulers and empires lies not in armies and emotions, but in the belief of men that they are inflexibly open and truthful and legal. So soon as a government departs from that standard, it ceases to be anything more than 'the gang in possession,' and its days are numbered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells sets a normative test for governments: perceived honesty and rule of law are core to durable legitimacy; covert encouragement of illegal violence or falsehood fatally undermines regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural political map vs. artificial diplomatic carving
rubrics_metrics.description: We have already pointed out that there must be a natural political map of the world which gives the best possible geographical divisions for human administrations... The diplomatists at Vienna evidently neither believed nor understood anything of the sort, and thought themselves as free to carve up the world...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political boundaries imposed without regard to natural social, racial, linguistic affinities create misfits that generate conflict; policy should account for organic political geography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of nationalism as exaggerated tribalism and source of conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential idea of nineteenth-century nationalism was the 'legitimate claim' of every nation to complete sovereignty... The flaw in this idea is that the affairs and interests of every modern community extend to the uttermost parts of the earth. A world of independent sovereign nations means... a world of perpetual injuries...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells treats nationalism as an over-stimulated tribal sentiment that, in a globally interdependent world, produces perpetual conflict rather than security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda and national symbols shape popular readiness for war
rubrics_metrics.description: Caricature and political cartoons played a large part in this elevation of the cult of these newer and bigger tribal gods... To the common man... it was made clear that instead of this being merely the result of the obstinacy and greed of two foreign offices, it was really a necessary part of a righteous inevitable gigantic struggle...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass media, symbolism, and caricature can mythologize international disputes, transforming governmental actions into perceived moral or divine struggles and thereby mobilizing support for war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education that fosters narrow loyalty undermines universal brotherhood
rubrics_metrics.description: The growing boy was exhorted to be 'loyal' to his school... 'loyal' to his nation and contemptuous and fierce towards other nations... His instinct for brotherhood was narrowed and debased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells identifies pedagogical cultivation of exclusive loyalties as contributing to militarism, xenophobia, and the erosion of broader human solidarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historian's scope: record small beginnings but avoid speculative 'may have beens'
rubrics_metrics.description: It may have been a merely temporary decline due to the need for a sloughing-off of the out-worn theology... Upon such 'may have beens' we can speculate here, but we cannot decide. History can deal with the small beginnings in the past of the great things of the present, but in the present only with what is plain and obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wells draws a methodological line: historians may note possible causes but should limit firm claims to demonstrable developments and concrete beginnings.
